::: {.lead}
The shuttle of *Star Dock* finally gets its controls. The first test is a
disaster: on a fast laptop the shuttle races, on an old one it crawls; it
flies faster diagonally; it always points to the right, even when it flies
up; it flies through the hangar walls; and the sprite is drawn in the wrong
place. Each problem has a mathematical fix that you already know: vectors
(lectures 2–3), angles (lecture 4) and transformations (lectures 5–7).
In this case study you build the movement of one 2D object, step by step,
and solve one part of it together with a team. Every section ends with a
short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary game-loop delta-time frame-rate-independence input-vector unit-vector velocity angular-speed atan2 surface-normal reflection-vector trs-matrix team-roles >}}

## 17.1 Motion per frame with Δt

The game loop moves the shuttle a little in every frame. The size of that
step must depend on the time of the frame (@fig-steps).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.1 — Motion per frame"}
Each frame takes $\Delta t$ seconds (1/60 s at 60 fps). With velocity
$\vec{v}$ (units per second):
$$\vec{p}_{\text{new}} = \vec{p} + \vec{v} \cdot \Delta t.$$
This is **frame-rate independence**: at 30, 60 or 144 fps the shuttle
covers the same distance per second.
:::

![The same second at 30 and at 60 fps.](images/frame-steps.png){#fig-steps width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.1 — 30 or 60 fps"}
Speed 6 units per second, to the right.

1. At 60 fps: each step is $6 \cdot \frac{1}{60} = 0.1$; 60 steps give
   6 units.
2. At 30 fps: each step is $6 \cdot \frac{1}{30} = 0.2$; 30 steps give
   6 units.
3. Without $\Delta t$ ("move 0.1 every frame"), the 30 fps laptop moves
   only 3 units per second.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="In game code"}
```csharp
void Update() {
    transform.position += (Vector3)(velocity * Time.deltaTime);
}
```
:::

**Turning works the same way.** An object that turns with the angular
speed ω (degrees per second) turns by **Δθ = ω × Δt** in each frame (lecture
9): a windmill at 180° per second turns by 180 × 1/60 = 3° per frame at 60
fps, and by 6° per frame at 30 fps.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Using a fixed step or a fixed angle per frame. The game then runs faster on
fast computers and slower on slow ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Δt"}
A meteor flies at 12 units per second. Compute its step per frame at 30,
60 and 120 fps, and check that each gives 12 units per second. Then: a
turret turns at 90° per second at 30 fps. How many degrees per frame?

*Your result:* three steps, three checks and one angle.

::: {.check}
30 fps: 12/30 = 0.4 (× 30 = 12); 60 fps: 0.2 (× 60 = 12); 120 fps: 0.1
(× 120 = 12). The turret: 90 × 1/30 = 3° per frame.
:::
:::

## 17.2 Input and diagonal movement

Keys or a stick give an **input vector** (@fig-diag).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.2 — Normalized input"}
Right gives (1, 0), up gives (0, 1); right + up gives (1, 1), which is
longer than 1 (about 1.4). To fly at the same speed in every direction,
**normalize** the input when its length is greater than 1:
$$\vec{d} = \frac{\text{input}}{|\text{input}|}, \qquad \vec{v} = \text{speed} \cdot \vec{d}.$$
A stick can give a length below 1 (half pushed): keep it, for slow
movement.
:::

![Diagonal input.](images/diagonal.png){#fig-diag width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.2 — The fast diagonal"}
1. Speed 5, keys right + up, input (1, 1): $\vec{v} = (5, 5)$, about 7 units
   per second: about 40 % too fast.
2. The game normalizes the input first: then the shuttle flies at 5 in every
   direction (Move Lab shows it).
3. A stick gives the raw input (3, 4), length 5. Normalized: (0.6, 0.8); with
   speed 10: $\vec{v} = (6, 8)$, length 10.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/move-lab.html" poster="sims/move-lab.png" title="Move Lab: fly the shuttle of Star Dock" height="820" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Normalizing (0, 0). A zero vector has no direction: dividing by its length
0 gives an error. Check the length first.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Diagonals"}
1. In **Move Lab**, fly ↗ with "normalize input" off and on. Write both
   speeds.
2. Compute the velocity for the raw stick input (−3, 4) and speed 10,
   normalized.

*Your result:* two speeds and one vector.

::: {.check}
Off: about 7 instead of 5 (too fast); on: 5. (−3, 4) has length 5:
(−0.6, 0.8) × 10 = **(−6, 8)**.
:::
:::

## 17.3 Facing the velocity

The shuttle should point where it flies (@fig-face).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.3 — Facing with atan2"}
If the sprite is drawn facing $+x$, its rotation angle is
$$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(v_y, v_x).$$
Turn only when the speed is not 0; otherwise keep the last angle.
:::

![Turn the ship to face its velocity.](images/facing.png){#fig-face width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.3 — Three directions"}
1. $\vec{v} = (5, 5)$: $\operatorname{atan2}(5, 5) = 45°$.
2. $\vec{v} = (0, 5)$: 90°. $\vec{v} = (-5, 0)$: 180°.
3. $\vec{v} = (0, 0)$: the shuttle stands still; it keeps its last angle.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing atan2(x, y) instead of atan2(y, x): the angle is then measured from
the y-axis, and the ship points the wrong way.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Facing"}
Compute the facing angle for $\vec{v} = (0, -2)$, $(4, -4)$ and $(-3, -3)$.

*Your result:* three angles.

::: {.check}
−90° (or 270°); −45° (or 315°); −135° (or 225°).
:::
:::

## 17.4 Bouncing off walls

When the shuttle hits a hangar wall, its velocity is reflected
(@fig-bounce).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.4 — Reflected velocity"}
With the unit normal $\vec{n}$ of the wall (pointing into the hangar):
$$\vec{v}\,' = \vec{v} - 2(\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n})\,\vec{n}.$$
The part of $\vec{v}$ along the wall stays; the part into the wall turns
around. (This is a perfect bounce, with bounciness e = 1.)
:::

![A bounce.](images/bounce.png){#fig-bounce width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.4 — Floor and wall"}
1. Floor, $\vec{n} = (0, 1)$, $\vec{v} = (4, -3)$: $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n} = -3$;
   $\vec{v}\,' = (4, -3) - 2(-3)(0, 1) = (4, 3)$.
2. Right wall, $\vec{n} = (-1, 0)$, $\vec{v} = (4, 3)$: $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n} =
   -4$; $\vec{v}\,' = (4, 3) - 2(-4)(-1, 0) = (-4, 3)$.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/bounce-lab.html" poster="sims/bounce-lab.png" title="Bounce Lab: reflect the velocity" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Turning both parts: $(4, -3) \to (-4, 3)$. Only the part along the normal
changes its sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Bounces"}
1. In **Bounce Lab**, check Example 17.4 with e = 1.
2. Compute the bounce of $\vec{v} = (-2, 5)$ on the ceiling, $\vec{n} = (0, -1)$.

*Your result:* the lab results and one vector.

::: {.check}
The lab gives (4, 3) and (−4, 3). Ceiling: $\vec{v} \cdot \vec{n} = -5$;
$\vec{v}\,' = (-2, 5) - 2(-5)(0, -1) = (-2, 5) + (0, -10) = $ **(−2, −5)**.
:::
:::

## 17.5 Drawing the sprite: local to world

The game knows the shuttle's position, angle and size; the sprite's corners
are stored in **local space**. A TRS transform puts them into the world
(@fig-trs).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 17.5 — The sprite's transform"}
For a corner $\vec{c}$ in local space: first **scale** (S), then
**rotate** (R) by the facing angle, then **translate** (T) to the
position:
$$\vec{c}_{\text{world}} = T \cdot R \cdot S \cdot \vec{c}$$
(lecture 7). In homogeneous coordinates this is one $3 \times 3$ matrix.
:::

![Local corners to world.](images/sprite-trs.png){#fig-trs width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 17.5 — The nose of the shuttle"}
Scale 2, angle 90°, position (5, 3).

1. Nose (1, 0) → S → (2, 0) → R(90°) → (0, 2) → T → **(5, 5)**.
2. Back (−0.5, 0.5) → (−1, 1) → (−1, −1) → **(4, 2)**.
3. Back (−0.5, −0.5) → (−1, −1) → (1, −1) → **(6, 2)**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Translating before rotating: the shuttle then circles around the origin
instead of turning on the spot.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · World corners"}
Compute the world corners of the shuttle with scale 1, angle 180° and
position (2, 4). The local corners are (1, 0), (−0.5, 0.5) and (−0.5, −0.5).

*Your result:* three points.

::: {.check}
R(180°) turns (x, y) into (−x, −y). Nose (1, 0) → (−1, 0) → **(1, 4)**;
(−0.5, 0.5) → (0.5, −0.5) → **(2.5, 3.5)**; (−0.5, −0.5) → (0.5, 0.5) →
**(2.5, 4.5)**.
:::
:::

## Team activity: the drone mission

::: {.callout-note title="Team activity · The drone mission (about 20 minutes)"}
**Mission.** A repair drone of *Star Dock* starts at (2, 1) with speed 4 and
the input ↑ (0, 1). After 2 seconds it hits the hangar ceiling
($\vec{n} = (0, -1)$, e = 1). Its sprite has scale 1.5.

**Team roles** (teams of three):

1. **Movement:** the velocity, the position after 2 s, and the step per frame
   at 60 fps.
2. **Facing and drawing:** the facing angle before the hit, and the world
   position of the nose (1, 0) at the start.
3. **Bounce:** the velocity after the ceiling, and the new facing angle.

Each member solves one part and **checks** the part of one other member.
Then the team presents its solution in two minutes: one slide or one page,
with every step.

**Individual alternative.** A student who works alone solves all three
parts in order, checks each part with **Move Lab** or **Bounce Lab**, and
hands in one page with the steps.

::: {.check}
Movement: $\vec{v} = (0, 4)$; after 2 s: (2, 1) + (0, 8) = (2, 9); step
4/60 ≈ 0.07 per frame. Facing: 90°; nose (1, 0) → (1.5, 0) → (0, 1.5) →
(2, 2.5). Bounce: (0, 4) → (0, −4); new facing −90°.
:::
:::

## Case study: Pilot Check

Before the shuttle may fly, the test pilots check six numbers of its
movement code: the step at 30 fps with the speed 6; what the code must do
with the input (1, 1); the facing angle of the velocity (−4, 4); the turn
per frame of a turret at 120° per second and 60 fps; the bounce of
(−3, 2) on the left wall; and the world position of a sprite corner (1, 0)
with scale 3, a turn of 90° and the position (4, 1). The Game challenge of
the interactive page uses these checks. In the mini-game below you choose
the right result for each one.

{{< sim file="sims/pilot-check.html" poster="sims/pilot-check.png" title="Pilot Check: six numbers of the movement code" kind="game" height="440" >}}

## Further reading

Dunn and Parberry, *3D Math Primer for Graphics and Game Development*, 2nd
ed. (2011), Chapters 2 and 5. Nystrom, *Game Programming Patterns* (2014),
the chapter "Game Loop" (free online).

## Exercises

1. Write the update rule for the position with Δt.
2. Speed 9, 30 fps: what is the step per frame?
3. Why is a game without Δt slower on a slow computer?
4. A wheel turns at 240° per second at 60 fps. How many degrees per frame?
5. Normalize the stick input (0, −2).
6. Speed 10 and the raw input (3, 4), normalized: what is the velocity?
7. Facing angle for $\vec{v} = (-1, 1)$?
8. Facing angle for $\vec{v} = (0, -3)$?
9. Reflect $\vec{v} = (3, -2)$ on the floor $\vec{n} = (0, 1)$.
10. Reflect $\vec{v} = (-5, 1)$ on the left wall $\vec{n} = (1, 0)$.
11. Scale 1, angle 90°, position (3, 3): where is the nose (1, 0)?
12. Why must the sprite be rotated before it is translated?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. $\vec{p} \mathrel{+}= \vec{v} \cdot \Delta t$.
2. $9 / 30 = 0.3$.
3. It moves the same step per frame, and a slow computer has fewer frames
   per second.
4. 240 × 1/60 = 4°.
5. (0, −1).
6. (0.6, 0.8) × 10 = (6, 8).
7. 135°.
8. −90° (or 270°).
9. $(3, 2)$.
10. $(5, 1)$.
11. (1, 0) → (0, 1) → (3, 4).
12. Otherwise it rotates around the origin of the world and moves away.
:::
